title: Building the Retrieval Pipeline
description: Parsing real-world documents, chunking specifically for RAG's dual requirements, embedding and indexing a corpus with proper metadata, and rewriting queries to improve retrieval.

lessons.title: Parsing Real-World Documents
lessons.description: Turn messy PDFs, tables, and HTML into clean text a RAG pipeline can actually use.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why document parsing is a genuine, non-trivial first step in a RAG pipeline.

sections.title: 📄 Real documents are messier than plain text
sections.content: Before chunking and embedding can happen, raw source documents (PDFs, Word docs, HTML pages, scanned images) need to be parsed into clean, usable text. This sounds simple but often isn't: PDFs can have multi-column layouts that get scrambled when extracted naively, tables need special handling to preserve their row/column structure as meaningful text, and scanned documents need OCR (optical character recognition) before there's any text to extract at all.

sections.title: 🎯 Parsing quality is a ceiling on everything downstream
sections.content:
If parsing garbles a table into a meaningless jumble of numbers, or scrambles a multi-column PDF's reading order, no amount of good chunking, embedding, or retrieval afterward can recover the information that was lost or corrupted at this very first step — parsing quality sets a hard ceiling on the whole pipeline's potential quality.

```python
# Conceptual: naive text extraction can scramble structure
# A two-column PDF page read naively might interleave
# text from both columns line-by-line, producing
# nonsensical sentences that were never adjacent in the original
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using the simplest available text-extraction tool without checking its output on your actual documents.** Different tools handle multi-column layouts, tables, and formatting very differently — verify against your real document types, not just simple test cases.

**Treating tables as if they were plain paragraphs.** A table's meaning depends on its row/column structure; naively flattening it into running text can destroy the information the table was organized to convey.

**Skipping OCR quality checks on scanned documents.** OCR errors introduce wrong characters or words directly into the text that gets embedded and retrieved — an OCR mistake becomes an invisible source of downstream retrieval and answer errors.

questions.question: Why is document parsing a nontrivial first step in a RAG pipeline, rather than a trivial formality?
options: Parsing is always simple and never introduces any real challenges
Real documents like PDFs with multi-column layouts, tables, or scanned images require careful handling to extract clean, correctly-ordered text — naive extraction can scramble or lose information
Parsing only matters for documents that contain no text at all
Document parsing has no effect on the quality of a RAG system's answers
questions.explanation: Turning messy real-world document formats into clean, correctly-structured text is genuinely difficult — multi-column layouts, tables, and scans each present their own extraction challenges that naive approaches can get badly wrong.

questions.question: Why does parsing quality set a ceiling on everything downstream in a RAG pipeline?
options: Parsing quality has no relationship to the quality of later pipeline stages
If parsing garbles or loses information at the very first step, no amount of good chunking, embedding, or retrieval afterward can recover information that was already corrupted or lost
Later pipeline stages always fix any errors introduced during parsing
Chunking and embedding happen before parsing, not after
questions.explanation: Since every later stage operates on the parsed text, information that's already scrambled or lost at the parsing step is permanently unavailable to every subsequent stage — parsing errors propagate forward and can't be corrected later.

questions.question: Why is naively flattening a table into plain running text a mistake during parsing?
options: Tables should always be flattened into plain text with no loss of meaning
A table's meaning depends on its row/column structure, so flattening it into unstructured running text can destroy the relationships the table was specifically organized to convey
Tables never contain any information worth preserving
Flattening tables always improves retrieval quality
questions.explanation: A table encodes meaning through its structure (which value belongs to which row and column) — collapsing that structure into plain text can turn a meaningful, organized dataset into a confusing, uninterpretable jumble of numbers and labels.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what four types of raw source documents does parsing need to handle?
options: PDFs, Word docs, HTML pages, and scanned images
Only plain text files with no other formats
Only spreadsheets and databases
Only audio and video files
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly lists PDFs, Word docs, HTML pages, and scanned images as the kinds of raw source documents that need to be parsed into clean, usable text.

questions.question: In this lesson's conceptual example, what specifically goes wrong when a two-column PDF is read naively?
options: Text from both columns can get interleaved line-by-line, producing nonsensical sentences that were never adjacent in the original
The PDF becomes completely unreadable with no text extracted at all
Only one of the two columns is extracted, with the other discarded
The columns are automatically detected and correctly separated every time
questions.explanation: The lesson's example explicitly describes naive extraction interleaving text from both columns, producing nonsensical sentences that weren't actually adjacent in the source.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say parsing quality sets 'a hard ceiling' on the whole pipeline's potential quality?
options: Because if parsing garbles or loses information at the first step, no amount of good chunking, embedding, or retrieval afterward can recover it
Because later pipeline stages always automatically correct any parsing errors
Because parsing has no actual effect on later stages of the pipeline
Because chunking and embedding happen before parsing in the pipeline order
questions.explanation: The lesson states that since every later stage builds on the parsed text, information lost or corrupted during parsing can never be recovered downstream.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend verifying a parsing tool's output against your actual document types rather than simple test cases?
options: Because different tools handle multi-column layouts, tables, and formatting very differently, so results on simple test cases may not reflect real performance
Because all parsing tools produce identical results regardless of document type
Because simple test cases always perfectly predict performance on real, complex documents
Because verifying against real documents is never actually necessary
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is using the simplest available extraction tool without checking its output on your actual documents, since tools vary significantly in how they handle real-world formatting.

questions.question: Why does this lesson single out OCR quality checks as important for scanned documents specifically?
options: Because OCR errors introduce wrong characters or words directly into the text that gets embedded and retrieved, becoming an invisible source of downstream errors
Because OCR is never actually necessary for scanned documents
Because OCR errors are always immediately obvious and easy to catch
Because scanned documents never contain any text worth extracting
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping OCR quality checks, since OCR mistakes silently corrupt the text before it even reaches chunking or embedding.

lessons.title: Chunking Strategies, Revisited for RAG
lessons.description: Apply chunking specifically to what makes a chunk retrievable and useful as generation context.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what makes a chunking strategy specifically good for RAG, beyond the general chunking concepts from earlier courses.

sections.title: 🎯 Two jobs, one chunk
sections.content: The LLM engineering and embeddings courses both covered chunking — but in a RAG context, a chunk has to do two things well at once: be embeddable as a coherent, focused unit (from the embeddings course's chunking-quality lesson) AND be directly usable as generation context once retrieved (a chunk needs enough surrounding information to actually answer a question, not just enough to be semantically distinct).

sections.title: 📏 Chunk size as a RAG-specific tradeoff
sections.content:
Too-small chunks may retrieve well (each one is very focused) but lack enough context for the generator to produce a complete, useful answer once inserted into the prompt. Too-large chunks may carry enough context but dilute the embedding (from the embeddings course) and waste token budget on irrelevant surrounding material. This is a genuinely RAG-specific balancing act, not just a generic 'pick a reasonable chunk size' decision.

```python
# Conceptual RAG-specific chunking check:
# - is this chunk focused enough to embed distinctly? (embeddings course)
# - does this chunk contain ENOUGH surrounding context to actually
#   answer a question about it, once retrieved and inserted into a prompt?
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Optimizing chunk size purely for embedding quality without checking generation usefulness.** A chunk that embeds beautifully but lacks enough surrounding context to actually answer a question fails at the generation stage, even if retrieval found it correctly.

**Using the exact same chunking parameters across very different document types.** A legal contract, a FAQ page, and a table of specifications may each need a different chunking approach to stay coherent and useful.

**Never testing chunking choices against actual end-to-end RAG answer quality, not just retrieval metrics alone.** Retrieval finding 'the right chunk' doesn't guarantee that chunk, once inserted into the prompt, actually contains enough for a good final answer.

questions.question: Why does a chunk in a RAG system need to satisfy two different requirements at once?
options: A chunk only ever needs to satisfy one requirement: being embeddable

It needs to be focused enough to embed as a coherent, distinct unit, while also containing enough surrounding context to actually be useful as generation context once retrieved and inserted into a prompt
Chunk requirements are identical to those covered in the embeddings course with no RAG-specific considerations
Chunks in RAG systems have no relationship to embedding quality at all
questions.explanation: A RAG chunk has to work well at two different stages: it needs to embed distinctly for good retrieval, and it needs to carry enough context to actually support answering a question once it's retrieved and used as generation input — a dual requirement specific to RAG.

questions.question: What is the risk of choosing chunks that are too small, purely to maximize embedding focus?
options: There is no risk; smaller chunks are always strictly better in every way
Very small chunks may embed well individually but lack enough surrounding context for the generator to produce a complete, useful answer once retrieved
Small chunks always contain too much irrelevant information
Chunk size has no effect on the usefulness of generation context
questions.explanation: While small, focused chunks can support precise retrieval, they can also be too narrow to give the generator enough surrounding information to actually construct a complete, useful answer — a tradeoff distinct from pure embedding quality.

questions.question: Why is testing chunking choices against end-to-end RAG answer quality more informative than testing retrieval metrics alone?
options: Retrieval metrics always perfectly predict final answer quality with no additional testing needed

Retrieval finding 'the right chunk' doesn't guarantee that chunk contains enough information to actually support a good final answer once used as generation context — the two are related but distinct measures of success
End-to-end testing and retrieval-only testing always produce identical conclusions
Answer quality has no relationship to which chunks were retrieved
questions.explanation: Since a technically 'correct' retrieved chunk can still lack the context needed for a complete answer, checking actual end-to-end answer quality catches problems that retrieval metrics alone (measuring whether the right chunk was found, not whether it was sufficient) would miss.

questions.question: According to this lesson, which two courses previously covered chunking before this lesson revisits it for RAG specifically?
options: The LLM engineering course and the embeddings course
The computer vision course and the math course
The SQL course and the transformers course
The Hugging Face course and the deep learning course
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly states that both the LLM engineering and embeddings courses covered chunking, and this lesson applies it specifically to RAG's dual requirements.

questions.question: In this lesson's conceptual code check, what two questions should a RAG-specific chunk satisfy?
options: Is the chunk focused enough to embed distinctly, and does it contain enough surrounding context to actually answer a question once retrieved
Is the chunk exactly 100 tokens long, and does it contain no punctuation
Is the chunk written in English, and does it avoid all technical terms
Is the chunk the first paragraph of a document, and does it contain a table
questions.explanation: The lesson's conceptual code comment lists these two specific checks: focus for embedding quality, and sufficiency of context for answering a question once retrieved.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe RAG chunk-size selection as 'a genuinely RAG-specific balancing act'?
options: Because too-small chunks may retrieve well but lack context for generation, while too-large chunks dilute the embedding and waste token budget — a tradeoff distinct from generic chunk-size advice
Because chunk size never actually matters in a RAG system
Because there is only one correct chunk size that works for every RAG application
Because this tradeoff is identical to a purely generic chunking decision with no RAG-specific element
questions.explanation: The lesson frames this as RAG-specific because it involves balancing embedding quality against generation usefulness simultaneously, not just a generic 'pick a reasonable size' choice.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against using identical chunking parameters across very different document types?
options: Because a legal contract, a FAQ page, and a table of specifications may each need a different chunking approach to stay coherent and useful
Because document type never actually affects the ideal chunking approach
Because every document type requires exactly the same chunk size to be effective
Because chunking parameters can never actually be varied by document type
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is applying the same chunking parameters everywhere, when different document types can need distinct approaches to remain coherent.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend testing chunking against end-to-end RAG answer quality, not just retrieval metrics alone?
options: Because retrieval finding 'the right chunk' doesn't guarantee that chunk, once inserted into the prompt, actually contains enough for a good final answer
Because retrieval metrics always perfectly predict final answer quality
Because end-to-end testing is never actually useful for evaluating chunking choices
Because retrieval metrics and answer quality are the exact same measurement
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is testing retrieval metrics alone, since a technically correct retrieved chunk can still be insufficient for generating a good final answer.

lessons.title: Embedding and Indexing the Corpus
lessons.description: Apply the embedding and indexing concepts from the previous course specifically to a RAG knowledge base.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the practical steps of turning a chunked document collection into a searchable RAG knowledge base.

sections.title: 🏗️ From chunks to a searchable index
sections.content: Once documents are parsed and chunked, each chunk is embedded (using an embedding model chosen with the criteria from the previous course) and stored in a vector index (HNSW, IVF, or a full vector database, also from the previous course) alongside metadata like source document, section, and any access-control information needed for filtering.

sections.title: 🏷️ Metadata is part of the knowledge base, not an afterthought
sections.content:
Storing rich metadata alongside each chunk's embedding (source document name, page number, last-updated date, access permissions) is what enables the metadata filtering and citation features covered elsewhere in this course — treating metadata as a first-class part of the index, not something to bolt on only if it turns out to be needed later.

```python
# Conceptual: what actually gets stored per chunk
vector_db.upsert(
    id=chunk_id,
    embedding=embed(chunk_text),
    metadata={
        "source_document": "refund_policy.pdf",
        "page": 3,
        "last_updated": "2026-01-15",
    },
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Embedding and indexing without storing enough metadata for later citation.** If the original source and location aren't stored alongside the chunk, providing an accurate citation later becomes impossible.

**Choosing an embedding model without considering the corpus's specific domain.** The embedding-model-choice lesson from the previous course applies directly here — a general-purpose model may underperform on a highly specialized knowledge base.

**Not planning for corpus updates from the start.** The indexing-workflow and staleness lessons from the embeddings course apply directly to a RAG knowledge base — documents will change, and the index needs a plan for staying current.

questions.question: What information should typically be stored alongside each chunk's embedding in a RAG knowledge base?
options: Only the raw embedding vector, with nothing else needed
Metadata like the source document, section or page, last-updated date, and access-control information, which enables filtering and accurate citation later
Only the chunk's exact character count
Metadata is never useful for a RAG system and can be safely omitted
questions.explanation: Storing metadata alongside each embedding is what enables the metadata filtering and citation capabilities a real RAG system needs — treating it as an essential part of the index rather than an optional add-on.

questions.question: Why does omitting source and location metadata make providing accurate citations impossible later?
options: Citations don't actually require knowing where information came from
Without storing the original source document and location alongside each chunk, there's no way to later trace a retrieved chunk back to a specific, verifiable source for citation purposes
Metadata has no relationship to a system's ability to cite sources
Citations can always be generated even without any stored metadata
questions.explanation: Accurate citation depends on knowing exactly where a piece of retrieved content came from — if that information was never captured and stored during indexing, there's nothing concrete to cite back to later.

questions.question: Why do the staleness and indexing-workflow concerns from the embeddings course apply directly to a RAG knowledge base?
options: RAG knowledge bases never change once they're initially indexed

A RAG knowledge base's source documents can change over time just like any other indexed data, so the same update strategies (upsert-on-change, batch re-indexing) are needed to keep the RAG index from going stale
Staleness is only a concern for non-RAG vector search applications
RAG systems automatically handle staleness without any explicit strategy
questions.explanation: A RAG knowledge base is just another instance of a vector-indexed collection, subject to the same staleness risk as any other — the update strategies covered generally in the embeddings course apply directly to keeping a RAG system's retrieved information current.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what specific metadata fields are stored alongside a chunk's embedding via vector_db.upsert?
options: source_document, page, and last_updated
Only the chunk's raw text with no other fields
Only a randomly generated unique identifier
The name of the embedding model used, with nothing else
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows vector_db.upsert storing metadata including source_document, page, and last_updated alongside the embedding.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what determines the vector index or database used to store a RAG corpus's embeddings?
options: Options like HNSW, IVF, or a full vector database, all covered in the previous (embeddings) course
A single mandatory index type with no alternatives
Whichever index type is randomly assigned at indexing time
Only a plain text file with no indexing structure at all
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly names HNSW, IVF, or a full vector database — all from the previous course — as the options for storing a RAG corpus's embeddings.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe metadata as 'part of the knowledge base, not an afterthought'?
options: Because storing rich metadata is what enables the metadata filtering and citation features covered elsewhere in this course
Because metadata has no functional purpose in a RAG system
Because metadata is only ever needed for aesthetic or display purposes
Because metadata can always be added later with no consequence to earlier design decisions
questions.explanation: The lesson frames metadata as first-class because it's specifically what enables later filtering and citation capabilities, not something to bolt on only if needed.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against choosing an embedding model without considering the corpus's specific domain?
options: Because a general-purpose model may underperform on a highly specialized knowledge base, echoing the embedding-model-choice lesson from the previous course
Because embedding model choice never actually affects performance on any corpus
Because general-purpose embedding models always outperform domain-specific ones
Because domain specificity is only relevant for chunking decisions, never embedding model choice
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake directly applies the previous course's embedding-model-choice lesson: a general-purpose model may underperform on a specialized domain-specific corpus.

questions.question: Why does this lesson stress planning for corpus updates 'from the start' rather than as an afterthought?
options: Because the indexing-workflow and staleness lessons from the embeddings course apply directly, and documents will change, requiring a plan for staying current
Because RAG knowledge bases never actually change once initially indexed
Because corpus update planning has no relationship to the earlier embeddings course
Because staleness is only a concern for non-RAG vector search systems
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is not planning for updates from the start, since the staleness concerns from the embeddings course apply directly to a RAG knowledge base's documents changing over time.

lessons.title: Query Formulation and Rewriting
lessons.description: Improve retrieval by transforming the user's raw question before searching with it.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why a user's raw question isn't always the best possible search query, and describe a technique for improving it.

sections.title: ❓ A user's question isn't always a good search query
sections.content: A user might ask something conversational, ambiguous, or dependent on earlier conversation turns ('What about the second one?') — none of which necessarily embeds well as a standalone search query. **Query rewriting** transforms the raw user input into a clearer, more self-contained, more retrieval-friendly form before it's used to search the knowledge base.

sections.title: 🔧 A few concrete rewriting techniques
sections.content:
**Conversation-aware rewriting** resolves references from earlier turns ('the second one' becomes the actual thing being referred to, using the conversation-state ideas from the LLM engineering course) into a standalone query. **Query expansion** adds related terms or rephrasing to increase the chance of matching relevant content phrased differently than the original question. **Decomposition** breaks a complex, multi-part question into several simpler sub-queries, each retrieved separately.

```python
# Conceptual: rewriting a context-dependent question into a standalone query
# conversation history: "Tell me about the Enterprise plan." -> "What's its price?"
# raw query "What's its price?" -> poor standalone search query
# rewritten query: "What is the price of the Enterprise plan?" -> good search query
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Sending the raw conversational query directly to the retriever without any rewriting.** This is a common, easy-to-miss cause of poor retrieval in multi-turn conversational RAG applications specifically.

**Over-rewriting and drifting from the user's actual intent.** A rewritten query needs to preserve what the user actually meant — an overly aggressive rewrite can search for something subtly different from the original question.

**Not evaluating rewriting's actual effect on retrieval quality.** Like any other pipeline change, query rewriting should be validated against the task-specific eval set (from the LLM engineering course) rather than assumed to always help.

questions.question: Why might a user's raw conversational question not work well as a direct search query for retrieval?
options: User questions are always perfectly suited as search queries with no issues
A raw question can be conversational, ambiguous, or dependent on earlier conversation turns (like 'What about the second one?'), which may not embed well or retrieve effectively as a standalone query
Search queries and user questions are always identical in every case
Retrieval quality has no relationship to how a query is phrased
questions.explanation: Conversational language often relies on context from earlier turns or is phrased in ways that don't stand alone well as a search query — this mismatch is exactly what query rewriting is designed to address before retrieval happens.

questions.question: What does conversation-aware query rewriting specifically address?
options: It has no relationship to conversation history at all
It resolves references from earlier conversation turns (like 'the second one') into a standalone, self-contained query that can be used effectively for retrieval
It always shortens every query to a single word
It replaces the retrieval step entirely with pure generation
questions.explanation: Since a follow-up question can depend heavily on earlier context, conversation-aware rewriting turns a context-dependent fragment into a complete, standalone query that retrieval can actually work with effectively.

questions.question: Why is over-rewriting a query a real risk, not just a theoretical concern?
options: Over-rewriting never actually changes what a query searches for
An overly aggressive rewrite can drift from what the user actually meant, causing the retriever to search for something subtly different from the original intended question
Rewriting a query always perfectly preserves the user's exact original intent with no risk of drift
Query rewriting is only ever applied to single-turn conversations
questions.explanation: Since rewriting reshapes the actual text used for retrieval, an overly aggressive transformation risks introducing a meaningful mismatch with the user's real intent — a genuine risk worth guarding against, not just a hypothetical edge case.

questions.question: In this lesson's conceptual example, how does the raw query 'What's its price?' get improved through rewriting?
options: It becomes the standalone query 'What is the price of the Enterprise plan?' by resolving the reference from conversation history
It is left completely unchanged since rewriting has no effect on pricing questions
It is shortened even further to just the word 'price'
It is translated into a different language before being used as a search query
questions.explanation: The lesson's example shows the context-dependent 'What's its price?' being rewritten into the standalone, retrieval-friendly 'What is the price of the Enterprise plan?' using conversation history.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what does 'query expansion' specifically do?
options: Adds related terms or rephrasing to increase the chance of matching relevant content phrased differently than the original question
Removes all but a single keyword from the original question
Translates the query into every supported language simultaneously
Deletes the original question and replaces it with a single generic query
questions.explanation: The lesson defines query expansion as adding related terms or rephrasings to improve the chance of matching relevantly-phrased content.

questions.question: What does this lesson call the technique of breaking a complex, multi-part question into several simpler sub-queries?
options: Decomposition
Consolidation
Truncation
Normalization
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly names 'decomposition' as breaking a complex, multi-part question into several simpler sub-queries, each retrieved separately.

questions.question: Why does this lesson call sending a raw conversational query directly to the retriever 'a common, easy-to-miss cause of poor retrieval'?
options: Because this specifically causes problems in multi-turn conversational RAG applications where questions depend on earlier turns
Because raw conversational queries always retrieve perfectly regardless of context dependence
Because this issue only ever occurs in single-turn, non-conversational applications
Because retrieval quality has no relationship to how a query is phrased
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping rewriting for conversational queries, which is specifically problematic for multi-turn conversational RAG applications.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend evaluating query rewriting against a task-specific eval set rather than assuming it always helps?
options: Because, like any other pipeline change, its actual effect on retrieval quality should be validated rather than assumed
Because query rewriting always helps in every single case with no exceptions
Because eval sets have no relevance to evaluating query rewriting specifically
Because rewriting can never actually be measured for its effect on retrieval
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is not evaluating rewriting's actual effect, echoing the LLM engineering course's task-specific eval set discipline applied here.
